title: Worksheet 12: Looping Through Strings
directions: Read the paragraph below carefully. Then answer all questions using ONLY the information in the paragraph. Circle the letter of the best answer.
paragraph: Because a string is made up of a sequence of individual characters, a loop can be used to move through a string one character at a time, checking or using each character in order, similar to how a loop can move through the items in a list. For example, a loop could go through the string "Robot" one character at a time, processing "R", then "o", then "b", then "o", then "t" in that exact order, running its code once for each of the 5 total characters in the string. A common use for looping through a string is counting how many times a specific character appears; for example, looping through the string "banana" and counting every time the letter "a" appears would result in a final count of 3, since the letter "a" appears at three separate positions within that specific word. Looping through strings is also commonly used for tasks like checking whether a string contains only letters and no numbers, or building a brand new string one character at a time based on certain rules applied to the original string.

questions.text: Based on the paragraph's example, looping through the string "banana" and counting every occurrence of the letter "a" results in a final count of 3. Using that same counting approach described in the paragraph, if a loop instead counted every occurrence of the letter "n" in the word "banana," approximately how many times would the letter "n" be counted, based on how many times it appears in that word?
questions.correct: 2 times, since the letter "n" appears at two separate positions in "banana"
distractors: 0 times, since "n" does not appear in "banana"
3 times, the same as the letter "a"
6 times, once for every letter in the word

questions.text: A programmer wants to loop through a string to check whether it contains only letters and no numbers, as mentioned in the paragraph. questions.correct: It would generally require examining each character, since any single character later in the string could turn out to be a number
